title: CJ McCollum on CP3, Westbrook Retiring, and Lillard's Return
htmlContent:
Atlanta Hawks guard CJ McCollum has spent 13 seasons sharing the floor with some of the best guards the NBA has produced. In a recent conversation with LandonBuford.com, McCollum spoke about the retirements of former Oklahoma City Thunder guards Chris Paul and Russell Westbrook, and about Damian Lillard's comeback from a torn Achilles tendon.

Two Hall of Famers Walk Away

Paul announced his retirement in February during NBA All-Star weekend, closing a 21-season career. Westbrook followed in August, ending an 18-year run that became legendary in Oklahoma City. McCollum, who battled both men for more than a decade, said their exits carried real weight.

"Two legends, two Hall of Famers that I had the pleasure of playing against and getting to know over the course of my career," McCollum said. "Sad to see them retire, but they had outstanding careers and did so much off the court, in all terms, and impacted people's lives."

The two point guards share a unique piece of Thunder history. They never played together in Oklahoma City. Instead, they were traded for one another in the summer of 2019, when Westbrook went to Houston and Paul arrived in OKC. Paul then led a Thunder team many had written off to the playoffs.

The Point God's Resume

Paul leaves the game as one of the most complete floor generals in league history. He was a 12-time All-Star, a two-time Olympic gold medalist and a member of the NBA's 75th Anniversary Team. He ranks second all-time in both assists and steals, trailing only John Stockton in each category.

His journey took him through New Orleans, the Clippers, Houston, Oklahoma City, Phoenix, Golden State and San Antonio, with a 2021 NBA Finals trip in Phoenix as the closest he came to a title. Off the court, he served as president of the National Basketball Players Association, a role McCollum later held himself.

Westbrook's Relentless Run

Westbrook brought a different kind of force to the position. The 2017 MVP retired as the NBA's all-time leader in triple-doubles with 209, and he led the league in assists three times. He also won All-Star Game MVP twice.

Even in his final season with the Sacramento Kings, he started 58 games and averaged 15.2 points, 6.7 assists and 5.4 rebounds.

An Impact Beyond Basketball

For McCollum, the conversation was never only about numbers.

"Their impact on the game is unquestioned," he said. "They made their mark and left the game in a better place. Those are two types of individuals that will leave even more impactful moments for people outside of basketball in the next half of their lives."

Both players built lasting work in their communities. Westbrook's Why Not? Foundation has focused on education and youth programs, and Paul has been a vocal advocate for HBCUs and player rights. McCollum, a longtime union leader and one of the league's more thoughtful voices, clearly sees that next chapter as part of their legacy.

Dame Is Back in Portland

McCollum's tone brightened when the subject turned to Lillard. The two formed one of the league's most dangerous backcourts in Portland from 2013 until McCollum was traded to New Orleans in 2022, highlighted by a run to the 2019 Western Conference Finals.

Lillard tore his left Achilles tendon in April 2025 during Milwaukee's first-round series against Indiana. The Bucks waived him that summer, and he returned to the Trail Blazers on a three-year deal before missing the entire 2025–26 season to rehab. He made his return in the preseason this month, scoring 15 points in a win over Golden State, and Portland opens its regular season against Phoenix.

"I'm excited to see Dame back doing his job," McCollum said. "He's going to have a great year. He's ready to go, and the game's in a better place when he's playing."

A Season of Transition

McCollum himself is coming off one of the most rewarding stretches of his career. After a midseason trade to Atlanta, the Hawks went 19-4 with him as a starter and pushed the eventual champion Knicks in the first round, earning him a one-year extension.

As one generation of point guards exits and another veteran star returns, McCollum's message was simple. Paul and Westbrook earned their flowers, and the NBA is a better place with Damian Lillard back on the floor.
